Frequently asked questions

FAQ

The questions I hear most often about learning to fly, with straight answers. Unless stated otherwise, everything below is about single-engine land airplanes (ASEL).

Many of the documents referenced here are free as PDFs from the FAA; printed versions cost a few dollars at any pilot shop. Use whichever form you will actually read.

Getting started

Where are your rates, policies and availability?

On the Rates & Policies page.

Do I need a medical certificate before I start?

Not for your first lessons, but you need one before you fly solo, and I recommend getting it early: if there is a medical issue to sort out, better to know before you have spent money on training. A third-class medical from an Aviation Medical Examiner (AME) is enough for private flying. Start the application at MedXPress, then see the AME. BasicMed is not an option for a brand-new pilot: it requires having held an FAA medical certificate at some point after July 14, 2006. Read: §61.23 and the FAA's medical certification page.

Do I need my own airplane?

No. Members of West Valley Flying Club fly club aircraft. If you own or rent an airplane, I can instruct in it — see Rates & Policies.

What should I buy before my first lesson?

Very little. A headset if you want your own (borrow one for the first flights), a logbook, and the free FAA handbooks. The full list is in the Library.

Private Pilot certificate

What does it take to earn a Private Pilot certificate?

The details are in Part 61, Subpart E. The summary:

  • Eligibility — be at least 17 (16 to solo as a student pilot); read, speak, write and understand English; hold a medical certificate.
  • Knowledge test — 60 questions, 2 hours 30 minutes, 70% to pass, taken at a testing center after an instructor's endorsement. The result is valid for 24 calendar months.
  • Ground instruction — the aeronautical knowledge areas in §61.105, logged with your instructor.
  • Flight experience — at least 40 hours (§61.109): 20 hours of training with an instructor and 10 hours solo, including 3 hours of cross-country training, 3 hours at night with a cross-country over 100 nm and ten full-stop landings, 3 hours by reference to instruments, 3 hours of checkride preparation within the two months before the test, 5 hours of solo cross-country including one flight of 150 nm with landings at three airports, and three solo full-stop landings at a towered airport.
  • Practical test — an oral exam and a flight with a Designated Pilot Examiner, flown to the Private Pilot ACS. Plan on most of a day.

Training runs in three phases, each ending in a milestone: first solo, solo cross-country, and the checkride.

Why do people say 40 hours when it takes more?

Forty is the regulatory minimum. In the Bay Area's busy, complex airspace most students need TBDtypical hours before they are ready for the practical test. That is not a reflection on the student; it is the depth of knowledge and skill the certificate demands here. The upside is that a pilot trained in this airspace is prepared to fly almost anywhere.

How long does it take?

It depends almost entirely on how often you fly. Training once or twice a week, most people finish in TBDtypical months. Flying three times a week is faster than three times as fast, because you forget less between lessons. Life, weather, vacation and scheduling all stretch the calendar.

How much does it cost?

TBDrealistic estimate and year. The total is made up of instructor time, aircraft rental for dual and solo flights, club membership, the knowledge test and examiner fees, and a modest amount for books and supplies. Some estimates you will see elsewhere are lower because they assume the 40-hour minimum.

The single most effective way to save money: show up prepared. Do the reading, have the airplane pre-flighted, get the weather briefing before I arrive. A prepared student learns more per hour, and there are fewer hours.

Which airplane should I train in?

TBDJack's recommendation and why

Whatever the airframe, I recommend training in an airplane with a glass cockpit such as the Garmin G1000. It is reliable, it gives you traffic and terrain awareness a six-pack panel cannot, and the workflow carries straight into your instrument rating and into the more capable airplanes you will fly later. Learning it from the start is easier than converting to it afterwards.

Is there a reading list?

Yes — in the Library.

Instrument rating

What does the instrument rating require?

  • Hold at least a Private Pilot certificate.
  • Pass the instrument knowledge test (60 questions, 2 hours 30 minutes, 70%).
  • Log 50 hours of cross-country time as pilot in command, at least 10 in airplanes.
  • Log 40 hours of actual or simulated instrument time, of which at least 15 hours are instrument training from an instructor, including one cross-country flight under IFR of at least 250 nm with an instrument approach at each airport and three different kinds of approaches.
  • Pass the practical test to the Instrument Rating ACS.

Read: §61.65.

How long does it take, and how much does it cost?

TBDtypical time and cost. The large variable is how much of the required instrument time you fly with me versus with a safety pilot.

How do I stay current afterwards?

Within the preceding six calendar months you need six instrument approaches, holding procedures, and intercepting and tracking courses. Let that lapse for another six months and you need an instrument proficiency check with an instructor before flying IFR again. Read: §61.57(c) and (d).

Everything else

Can I use BasicMed instead of an FAA medical?

If you have held an FAA medical at any point since July 14, 2006, possibly yes. BasicMed lets you fly certain aircraft with up to six occupants, below 18,000 ft and 250 knots, with a physician's exam every four years and an online course every two. Read: the FAA's BasicMed page.

What is a flight review, and do I need one?

Every pilot needs one every 24 calendar months to act as pilot in command: at least an hour of ground and an hour of flight with an instructor. Read: §61.56.
